feedback.problem: Given that the polynomial $f(x)=2{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+7x-6$ has one of its roots in the interval $(0,\frac{3}{2}),$ find the sum of the distinct real roots of $f(x).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-6$ and the leading coefficient is $2.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-6}{\text{factor of }2}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm \frac{1}{2},\,\pm \frac{3}{2},\,\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 6
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(0,\frac{3}{2}),$ are $\frac{1}{2}$ and $1.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-\frac{1}{2})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | $2$ | $9$ | $7$ | $-6$ |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $5$ | $6$ |
|  | $2$ | $10$ | $12$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x-\frac{1}{2})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x-\frac{1}{2})(2{x}^{2}+10x+12).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-\frac{1}{2})(2{x}^{2}+10x+12) \\  & =2(x-\frac{1}{2})({x}^{2}+5x+6) \\  & =2(x-\frac{1}{2})(x+2)(x+3)\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=\frac{1}{2},-2,-3.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
\frac{1}{2}-2-3=-\frac{9}{2}.
$$
